{{Short description|Endomorphism preserving the inner product}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
{{other uses|Transformation (mathematics) (disambiguation)}}
{{More citations needed|date=November 2025}}
In mathematics, a '''unitary transformation''' is a [[linear isomorphism]] that preserves the [[inner product]]: the inner product of two vectors before the transformation is equal to their inner product after the transformation.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hazewinkel |first=Michiel |author-link=Michiel Hazewinkel |title=Encyclopaedia of Mathematics |volume=9 |date=1993 |publisher=[[Kluwer Academic Publishers]] |isbn=978-1-55608-008-1 |page=337 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Encyclopaedia_of_Mathematics/1ttmCRCerVUC}}</ref>

==Formal definition==
More precisely, a '''unitary transformation''' is an [[isometry|isometric isomorphism]] between two [[inner product space]]s (such as [[Hilbert space]]s). In other words, a ''unitary transformation'' is a [[bijective function]]
:<math>U : H_1 \to H_2</math>
between two inner product spaces, <math>H_1</math> and <math>H_2,</math> such that 
:<math>\langle Ux, Uy \rangle_{H_2} = \langle x, y \rangle_{H_1} \quad \text{ for all } x, y \in H_1.</math>
It is a [[linear isometry]], as one can see by setting <math>x=y.</math>

==Unitary operator==
In the case when <math>H_1</math> and <math>H_2</math> are the same space, a unitary transformation is an [[automorphism]] of that Hilbert space, and then it is also called a [[unitary operator]].

==Relation to unitary matrices==
In [[complex coordinate space]] <math>\Complex^n</math> unitary transformations always have the shape

:<math>f \colon \Complex^n \to \Complex^n, \, x \mapsto U \cdot x</math>,

where  <math>U \in \Complex^{n \times n}</math> is a [[unitary matrix]], and the dot before the vector is the matrix-vector-product.

This matrix <math display="inline">U</math> satisfies <math display="inline">UU^* = I</math> <ref>{{cite journal |author=Fasi, Massimiliano; Robol, Leonardo |title=Sampling the eigenvalues of random orthogonal and unitary matrices |journal=Linear Algebra and its Applications |date=1 July 2021 |volume=620 |pages=297–321 |doi=10.1016/j.laa.2021.02.031|arxiv=2009.11515 }}</ref>.


==Antiunitary transformation==
A closely related notion is that of '''[[antiunitary]] transformation''', which is a bijective function

:<math>U:H_1\to H_2\,</math>

between two [[complex number|complex]] Hilbert spaces such that 

:<math>\langle Ux, Uy \rangle = \overline{\langle x, y \rangle}=\langle y, x \rangle</math> 

for all <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> in <math>H_1</math>, where the horizontal bar represents the [[complex conjugate]].
